questions.stem:
In the following reactions, P, Q, R, and S are the major products.
CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂CN —(i) PhMgBr, then H₃O⁺ (ii) PhMgBr, then H₂O→ P
Ph–H + CH₃COCl —(i) anhyd. AlCl₃ (ii) PhMgBr, then H₂O→ Q
CH₃CH₂COCl —(i) ½ (PhCH₂)₂Cd (ii) PhMgBr, then H₂O→ R
PhCH₂CHO —(i) PhMgBr, then H₂O (ii) CrO₃, dil. H₂SO₄ (iii) HCN (iv) H₂SO₄, Δ→ S
The correct statement(s) about P, Q, R, and S is(are)

options.text: Both P and Q have asymmetric carbon(s).
Both Q and R have asymmetric carbon(s).
Both P and R have asymmetric carbon(s).
P has asymmetric carbon(s), S does not have any asymmetric carbon.

questions.solution: P: PhMgBr adds to the nitrile and hydrolysis gives the ketone CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂COPh; a second PhMgBr gives CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂C(OH)Ph₂, whose C-3 (H, CH₃, C₂H₅, CH₂–) is asymmetric. Q: Friedel–Crafts acylation gives acetophenone and PhMgBr then gives Ph₂C(OH)CH₃, which carries two identical phenyls and is achiral. R: the organocadmium reagent stops at the ketone CH₃CH₂COCH₂Ph; PhMgBr gives CH₃CH₂C(OH)(Ph)CH₂Ph with four different groups, so it is chiral. S: PhCH₂CH(OH)Ph is oxidised to PhCH₂COPh, HCN gives the cyanohydrin, and hot H₂SO₄ hydrolyses CN to COOH and dehydrates it to PhCH=C(Ph)COOH, which has no asymmetric carbon. Hence (C) and (D).

check.note: Two independent solutions agree; the official key is not in the archived paper

questions.stem:
Consider the following reaction scheme and choose the correct option(s) for the major products Q, R and S.
Styrene —(i) B₂H₆ (ii) NaOH, H₂O₂, H₂O→ P —(i) CrO₃, H₂SO₄ (ii) Cl₂, Red phosphorus (iii) H₂O→ Q
P —(i) SOCl₂ (ii) NaCN (iii) H₃O⁺, Δ→ R —conc. H₂SO₄→ S

options.text: Q = PhCH(Cl)COOH; R = PhCH₂CH₂CONH₂; S = 3-(4-sulfophenyl)propanamide, HO₃S–C₆H₄–CH₂CH₂CONH₂ (para)
Q = PhCH(Cl)COOH; R = PhCH₂CH₂COOH; S = indan-1-one
Q = PhCH₂COCl; R = PhCH₂CH₂COOH; S = indan-1-one
Q = PhCH₂COCl; R = PhCH₂CH₂CONH₂; S = 3-(4-sulfophenyl)propanamide, HO₃S–C₆H₄–CH₂CH₂CONH₂ (para)

questions.solution: Hydroboration–oxidation of styrene gives the anti-Markovnikov alcohol PhCH₂CH₂OH (P). CrO₃/H₂SO₄ oxidises P to PhCH₂COOH, and Cl₂/red P (HVZ) followed by water gives PhCH(Cl)COOH (Q); the acid chloride is only an intermediate. SOCl₂ converts P to PhCH₂CH₂Cl, NaCN gives the nitrile and acidic hydrolysis gives PhCH₂CH₂COOH (R), an acid, not an amide. Conc. H₂SO₄ effects intramolecular Friedel–Crafts acylation of R to indan-1-one (S). Only (B) fits.

check.note: Two independent solutions agree; the official key is not in the archived paper

questions.stem:
In the given reaction scheme, P is a phenyl alkyl ether, Q is an aromatic compound; R and S are the major products.
P —HI→ Q —(i) NaOH (ii) CO₂ (iii) H₃O⁺→ R —(i) (CH₃CO)₂O (ii) H₃O⁺→ S
The correct statement about S is

options.text: It primarily inhibits noradrenaline degrading enzymes.
It inhibits the synthesis of prostaglandin.
It is a narcotic drug.
It is ortho-acetylbenzoic acid.

questions.solution: HI cleaves an aryl alkyl ether at the alkyl–O bond, so Q is phenol (plus an alkyl iodide). Kolbe–Schmitt carboxylation of sodium phenoxide with CO₂ followed by acidification gives salicylic acid (R). Acetylation of the phenolic OH with acetic anhydride gives acetylsalicylic acid, aspirin (S). Aspirin is a non-narcotic analgesic that works by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis; it is o-acetoxybenzoic acid, not o-acetylbenzoic acid.

check.note: Two independent solutions agree; the official key is not in the archived paper

questions.stem:
The total number of sp² hybridised carbon atoms in the major product P (a non-heterocyclic compound) of the following reaction is ___.
NC–CH(CN)–CH(CN)–CN —(i) LiAlH₄ (excess), then H₂O (ii) Acetophenone (excess)→ P
questions.solution: Excess LiAlH₄ reduces all four C≡N groups to CH₂NH₂, giving (H₂NCH₂)₂CH–CH(CH₂NH₂)₂. With excess acetophenone each primary amine condenses to an imine, –CH₂–N=C(CH₃)Ph; the product is stated to be non-heterocyclic, so no cyclic aminal forms. Each imine unit contributes one sp² C=N carbon and six aromatic carbons, 7 in all, and the four units give 4 × 7 = 28.

check.note: Two independent solutions agree; the official key is not in the archived paper

questions.stem:
Match the reactions in List-I with the features of their products in List-II and choose the correct option.
List-I
(P) (−)-1-Bromo-2-ethylpentane (single enantiomer) —aq. NaOH, SN2 reaction→
(Q) (−)-2-Bromopentane (single enantiomer) —aq. NaOH, SN2 reaction→
(R) (−)-3-Bromo-3-methylhexane (single enantiomer) —aq. NaOH, SN1 reaction→
(S) the bromide shown (single enantiomer) —aq. NaOH, SN1 reaction→
List-II
(1) Inversion of configuration
(2) Retention of configuration
(3) Mixture of enantiomers
(4) Mixture of structural isomers
(5) Mixture of diastereomers
questions.solution: (P) The SN2 attack happens at C-1 (CH₂Br), not at the stereocentre C-2, so the configuration of C-2 is retained → (2). (Q) SN2 at the stereocentre C-2 proceeds by backside attack → inversion (1). (R) SN1 at the tertiary stereocentre goes through a planar carbocation, giving both enantiomers of 3-methylhexan-3-ol → (3). (S) SN1 scrambles only the carbon bearing Br, while the other stereocentre (CH(CH₃)) is untouched, so the two products are diastereomers → (5). This is option (B).

check.note: Two independent solutions agree; the official key is not in the archived paper

questions.stem:
The major products obtained from the reactions in List-II are the reactants for the named reactions mentioned in List-I. Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct option.
List-I
(P) Etard reaction
(Q) Gattermann reaction
(R) Gattermann-Koch reaction
(S) Rosenmund reduction
List-II
(1) Acetophenone —Zn-Hg, HCl→
(2) Toluene —(i) KMnO₄, KOH, Δ (ii) SOCl₂→
(3) Benzene —CH₃Cl, anhyd. AlCl₃→
(4) Aniline —NaNO₂/HCl, 273-278 K→
(5) Phenol —Zn, Δ→
questions.solution: The Etard reaction (CrO₂Cl₂) needs toluene, made from benzene by Friedel–Crafts methylation (3). The Gattermann reaction (Cu/HX on ArN₂⁺) needs a diazonium salt, made by diazotising aniline at 273–278 K (4). The Gattermann–Koch reaction (CO/HCl, AlCl₃) needs benzene, obtained by distilling phenol with zinc dust (5). Rosenmund reduction needs an acid chloride, and toluene → benzoic acid → benzoyl chloride gives it (2). Clemmensen reduction of acetophenone (1) gives ethylbenzene, which is not needed. Answer (D).

check.note: Two independent solutions agree; the official key is not in the archived paper
